extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers interested in media freedom and censorship in the Middle East
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive overview of censorship practices, laws, and tactics used by Middle Eastern governments to control media and internet information flow, with country examples (Egypt, Qatar, Bahrain, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of censorship (retain governmental control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship is a policy used by governments to retain control over their people by preventing the public from viewing information considered by the republic as holding the potential to incite a rebellion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the rationale behind censorship policies: restricting access to potentially destabilizing information to maintain public order and regime stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal restrictions and direct control of ISPs
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first ways is for the government to place legal restrictions on the internet service providers or exhibit direct control over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments may compel ISPs by law or ownership to block, filter, or otherwise control traffic; legal frameworks can mandate compliance and provide enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking specific websites and media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Through this control, the government blocks certain websites or media (such as pictures, videos, and news articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Website and content blocking targets particular URLs, platforms, or pieces of media deemed controversial; examples include blocking news sites and independent outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance and monitoring of internet use
rubrics_metrics.description: The government ... is even able to place surveillance over certain sources. Under surveillance technology, authorities can block and monitor internet traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveillance is used both for intelligence/gathering and as a means to identify and then block or punish content creators and consumers; often paired with filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlawing or discouraging controversial media corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The government may outlaw, or even make informal requests discouraging the existence of controversial media corporations in their countries, in order to prevent the spread of ideas proposed by said companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and informal pressure (economic, legal, administrative) can be used to limit media actors' presence or operation in-country, reducing plurality of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network manipulation tactics (throttling and shutdowns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques include slowing down Internet speeds to prevent the spread of pictures and videos, ... and Egypt completely shut down the Internet for five days during the period of the most unrest in January 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics range from bandwidth throttling to full national or localized internet shutdowns used during crises to curb communication and information dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest, detention, and criminal prosecution of journalists and online activists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters Without Borders states ... at least 199 of those engaged in informing the public were arrested in 2011. Several journalists, citizen-journalists, and bloggers have been detained and sentenced to prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminalizing reporting and online activism—through arrests, trials, and prison sentences—serves as both punishment and deterrent; frequently used alongside content-control measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious / Shariah-based limits on expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech and right to the access of information in the Middle East is governed by Islamic principles ... people have the right to express their thoughts as long as it is within the limits of the Shariah law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions, Shariah-derived norms define permissible expression; authorities and jurists interpret religious limits to justify censorship and content restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egypt: Anti-Crime and Information Technology Crimes Law (2018) - hacking and publication limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anti-Crime and Information Technology Crimes Law was ratified on August 18, 2018 in Egypt. There will be penalties if one hacks government systems. The law prohibits any information regarding the police or military being published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific legal prohibitions include criminalizing unauthorized access to government systems and restricting publication of information about security forces; these expand prosecutorial grounds for online speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egypt: regulating social media as media outlets (threshold-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Egyptian parliament passed a law that treats social media accounts with more than 5,000 followers as media outlets. This means that they are subject to persecution if they publish fake news or break the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follower-count thresholds or similar metrics can be used to extend media regulations and liabilities to individual accounts and citizen-journalists, increasing state control over online speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content blocking on grounds of national security or economic threat
rubrics_metrics.description: This cybercrime law allows authorities to block content that is a threat to national security or economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad public-interest justifications (national security, economic stability) are codified as grounds for content removal or blocking, often with vague definitions enabling wide application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar: criminalization for harming national interests or public opinion (Article 136)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 136 allows for the imprisonment of anyone who publishes or broadcasts content which harm national interests or public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory offenses that criminalize 'harm' to national interests/public opinion permit prosecution for a wide range of communications; enforcement can be used against journalists and broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar: institutional censorship via a publications/censorship committee (Law on Printing and Publication 1979)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 62 deals with the creation of a committee in Qatar to control the censorship policies; representatives will be chosen from Ministries of Education, Interior, Labor and Social Affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative bodies with cross-ministerial membership are empowered to oversee and implement censorship, institutionalizing pre-publication review and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar: pre-publication review of artistic works (Article 63)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 63 entails how artistic works need to be reviewed before they are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring prior review of creative content enables authorities to screen and censor art, film, literature, and other cultural outputs before public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar: content compliance standards enforced by Department of Publications (Article 64)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 64 states that the Department of Publications and Publishing may direct the Censorship Committee and observe that technical, social, religious, ethical and cultural traditions are being followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content is evaluated for conformity with a set of social/religious/ethical/cultural norms; these broad categories provide discretionary grounds for censorship decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qatar: surprise inspections and on-site enforcement (Article 65)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 65 states that sudden inspections can occur in cinemas and other locations in Qatar to make sure that films, ads and shows are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-site inspections and enforcement enable immediate removal or sanctioning of content seen as inappropriate, extending censorship beyond digital spaces into physical venues.
